title: How loan payments pay down a balance: amortization

national.document: 2021 National Standards for Personal Financial Education (CEE and Jump$tart)
national.learning_target: Explain how loan payments are applied to interest and principal (amortization)
national.outcome_code_status: to verify against the official document

new_jersey.performance_expectation_status: strand-level alignment; individual 9.1.12 performance expectations to verify

sections.skill: Split a loan payment into interest and principal and follow the balance

questions.prompt: Dev has a $10,000 loan at 6% APR with a $193.33 monthly payment. How much of the FIRST payment is interest?
questions.intro: Amortization is paying off a loan with regular payments. Each payment first covers that month's interest (balance × monthly rate); the rest reduces the principal. Early payments are mostly interest; later payments are mostly principal.
questions.topic: How loan payments pay down a balance: amortization

misconceptions.C: Treats the whole payment as interest

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Dev's first payment of $193.33 includes $50.00 of interest. How much reduces the principal, and what is the new balance?
questions.intro: Principal paid = payment − interest. New balance = old balance − principal paid.
questions.topic: How loan payments pay down a balance: amortization

misconceptions.A: Treats the whole payment as principal

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Dev's balance after one payment is $9,856.67 at 6% APR (0.5% per month). How much interest is in the SECOND payment (nearest cent)?
questions.intro: Each month, interest is charged on the balance that remains after the previous payment.
questions.feedback: $9,856.67 × 0.005 ≈ $49.28. As the balance falls, interest falls and more of each payment goes to principal.
questions.topic: How loan payments pay down a balance: amortization
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Over the life of an amortizing loan with equal payments, how does the INTEREST part of each payment change?

choices.text: It gets larger over time
It stays the same every month
It gets smaller over time
It is zero until the last year

questions.intro: In an amortizing loan, each payment's interest is figured on a balance that keeps shrinking.
questions.feedback: Interest is figured on a shrinking balance, so the interest part falls and the principal part rises.
questions.topic: How loan payments pay down a balance: amortization
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: An amortization schedule shows payment 1: interest $50.00, principal $143.33. What will the LAST payment of the loan be mostly?

choices.text: Principal
Interest
Fees
Taxes

questions.intro: An amortization schedule lists each payment's interest part, principal part, and remaining balance. Interest is always figured on the balance still owed.
questions.feedback: By the end, the balance is small, so almost all of the payment is principal.
questions.topic: How loan payments pay down a balance: amortization

misconceptions.D: Not part of a loan payment

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

sections.skill: Interest is charged on the balance still owed
sections.relationship: Amortization depends on recalculating interest on the remaining balance each month.

questions.prompt: Dev adds $50 extra to principal in month 1 of his $10,000 loan at 0.5% per month. How much interest does this save in month 2?
questions.intro: An extra payment goes straight to principal. That lowers the balance, so every later month's interest is a little smaller, and the loan ends sooner.
questions.feedback: $50 × 0.005 = $0.25 less interest in month 2, and similar savings every month after.
questions.topic: How loan payments pay down a balance: amortization

misconceptions.D: Treats the extra payment as interest saved

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: On an amortizing loan with no prepayment penalty, what happens to the loan when extra principal is paid each month?

choices.text: It is paid off sooner, and total interest falls
The required monthly payment goes up automatically
The interest rate rises
Nothing changes

questions.correct_answer: It is paid off sooner, and total interest falls
questions.intro: Extra payments on principal reduce the balance faster than the schedule, so later payments carry less interest.
questions.feedback: Lower balance → less interest → earlier payoff.
questions.topic: How loan payments pay down a balance: amortization
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: When making an extra payment, what instruction should a borrower give the lender?

choices.text: Apply it to next month's interest only
Hold it as a credit for fees
Refund it at the end of the year
Apply the extra amount to principal

questions.correct_answer: Apply the extra amount to principal
questions.intro: Some lenders apply extra money to future payments unless told otherwise. Telling them to apply it to principal reduces the balance right away.
questions.feedback: Directing it to principal ensures the balance and future interest fall.
questions.topic: How loan payments pay down a balance: amortization
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.topic: How loan payments pay down a balance: amortization

questions.prompt: Which statement about extra payments is TRUE for most amortizing loans with no prepayment penalty?

choices.text: Extra payments only help in the final year
Extra payments increase the total interest paid on the loan
Extra dollars paid early save more than late ones
Extra payments are not allowed

questions.correct_answer: Extra dollars paid early save more than late ones
questions.intro: The earlier principal is reduced, the more months of interest are avoided.
questions.feedback: Early extra principal avoids interest for many more months.
questions.topic: How loan payments pay down a balance: amortization
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Row 12 of a schedule shows: payment $193.33, interest $44.22, principal $149.11, balance $8,694.98. How much of payment 12 reduced the debt?
questions.intro: Each row of an amortization schedule shows the payment, its interest part, its principal part, and the balance after the payment.
questions.feedback: The principal part, $149.11, reduced the debt.
questions.topic: How loan payments pay down a balance: amortization

questions.prompt: A schedule row shows: interest $44.22, principal $149.11, balance $8,694.98 after the payment. What was the balance before that payment?
questions.intro: Balance before payment = balance after payment + principal part.
questions.topic: How loan payments pay down a balance: amortization
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: A schedule shows interest of $44.22 on a balance of $8,844.09 for one month. What monthly rate is that (nearest tenth of a percent)?
questions.intro: Monthly rate = interest for the month ÷ balance.
questions.topic: How loan payments pay down a balance: amortization
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: In a 60-payment schedule for $10,000 at 6% APR, the total of the interest column is about $1,599.80. What is the total of the principal column?
questions.intro: Over the full life of a loan, the principal parts of all payments add up to the amount borrowed.
questions.feedback: The principal parts repay exactly the amount borrowed.
questions.topic: How loan payments pay down a balance: amortization

questions.prompt: Which schedule feature shows that a loan is "front-loaded" with interest?

choices.text: The balance rises each month
Every payment has an equal amount of interest in it
Interest parts are largest in the first payments
The last payment is all interest

questions.correct_answer: Interest parts are largest in the first payments
questions.intro: "Front-loaded" means more of something comes at the beginning.
questions.feedback: Early balances are largest, so early payments contain the most interest.
